{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-in-s","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"2382f51dcacd203b46d6cd0ad4891931d7f0ad943ba92c9c37c7e9d130ab0600","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-in-class-std:lineage:28","source_registry_sha256":"2800087d52ca58455ac6dac735a6e1bd60a4442f9e09c2356d96bd9ed8102504","source_liveness_sha256":"4d2b75b9a10fb774f53fb2d906a3a7a7f75f5e9387f8b4ddcd423e9b7828d59b"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C2"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C2","chunk_id":"C2.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Safe operation part one confusables and continuation","heading":"C2 — Confusable pairs and knowledge-graph hints: rural versus urban limits, high versus low beams, roundabouts versus traffic circles, skids, and continuation facts on lane use, weather, fuel, drowsiness, texting, rural roads and interstates","learner_facing":false,"markdown":"## C2 — Confusable pairs and knowledge-graph hints: rural versus urban limits, high versus low beams, roundabouts versus traffic circles, skids, and continuation facts on lane use, weather, fuel, drowsiness, texting, rural roads and interstates
Confusable pairs from the first half of the safe-operation chapter, followed by continuation facts the main list did not hold; each block ties to one handbook page, and hint metadata sits only in the trailing line of a block.

FACT_ID: sec07-R01 | anchor: A04
A roundabout carries only counterclockwise traffic, while a traffic circle may carry traffic in both directions and may use stop signs instead of yield signs on its approaches. [A04]
Why it matters: group intersections; confusable roundabout versus traffic circle.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec07-R02 | anchor: A08
The low-beam rule uses 500 feet for an oncoming vehicle but only 200 feet when you are following another vehicle. [A08]
Why it matters: group headlights; confusable facing versus following distance.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0049]

FACT_ID: sec07-R03 | anchor: A06
The skid steps are the same for front-wheel-drive and rear-wheel-drive cars; what changes the technique is whether the car has conventional or anti-lock brakes. [A06]
Why it matters: group skids; confusable drive type versus brake type.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec07-R04 | anchor: A05
A school bus off interstates and state highways is limited to 40 miles per hour, while on an interstate or highway its limit is 60 miles per hour or the posted limit. [A05]
Why it matters: group speed limits; confusable school bus road types.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec07-R05 | anchor: A01
On the highway, slower vehicles should keep right, leaving the left lane for faster or passing traffic. [A01]
Why it matters: group lane use; difficulty low.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec07-R06 | anchor: A01
Before changing lanes, check the lane ahead, check mirrors for anyone about to pass you, glance over your shoulder at the blind spot, signal, then move over smoothly. [A01]
Why it matters: group lane changes; sequence item.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec07-R07 | anchor: A01
Weaving in and out of lanes greatly raises the risk of a crash. [A01]
Why it matters: group lane changes; difficulty low.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec07-R08 | anchor: A02
Stay in the passing lane until the vehicle you passed shows in your rearview mirror, then signal before moving back. [A02]
Why it matters: group passing; sequence item.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec07-R09 | anchor: A03
Center lanes reserved for left turns are usually marked with CENTER LANE ONLY signs or pavement arrows, though some have neither. [A03]
Why it matters: group turning; difficulty medium.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0044]

FACT_ID: sec07-R10 | anchor: A03
At a median U-turn or J-turn intersection, the left turn is banned at the intersection itself, so drivers go through and make a U-turn at a median opening ahead. [A03]
Why it matters: group turning; difficulty high.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0044]

FACT_ID: sec07-R11 | anchor: A04
In a multi-lane roundabout, pick your lane before entering and do not change lanes while circulating. [A04]
Why it matters: group roundabouts; difficulty medium.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec07-R12 | anchor: A04
When the driver ahead signals a turn or slows as if to turn, slow down and be ready to stop. [A04]
Why it matters: group following; difficulty low.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec07-R13 | anchor: A04
Going over the speed limit reduces your ability to steer around curves and objects, lengthens emergency stopping distance and makes crashes more severe. [A04]
Why it matters: group speed; difficulty low.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec07-R14 | anchor: A05
At 55 miles per hour a vehicle covers about 80.7 feet each second, compared with about 51.3 feet at 35 and 102.7 feet at 70. [A05]
Why it matters: group stopping; numbers for scenario items.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec07-R15 | anchor: A05
Stopping ability depends on vehicle weight, brakes, tires, pavement condition and slickness, and the grade of the road. [A05]
Why it matters: group stopping; difficulty medium.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec07-R16 | anchor: A05
Driving at or above the posted limit is even more dangerous in bad weather, on icy roads, with worn tires, with unsafe vehicle conditions or when physically impaired. [A05]
Why it matters: group speed; difficulty low.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec07-R17 | anchor: A06
Rollover crashes make up nearly one-third of passenger vehicle deaths; keeping control of the vehicle is the biggest factor in avoiding one, and badly inflated or worn tires undermine that control. [A06]
Why it matters: group rollover; difficulty medium.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec07-R18 | anchor: A06
Rollovers are more likely on undivided two-way roads or divided roads without barriers, and a car leaving a rural road can roll when it hits a ditch, an embankment or soft soil. [A06]
Why it matters: group rollover; link to rural roads.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec07-R19 | anchor: A06
Fuel use climbs steadily above 45 miles per hour, and cars and light trucks use roughly 50 percent more fuel at 75 than at 55. [A06]
Why it matters: group fuel economy; difficulty low.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec07-R20 | anchor: A06
Several short trips from a cold start can burn twice as much fuel as one longer trip covering the same distance. [A06]
Why it matters: group fuel economy; difficulty low.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec07-R21 | anchor: A07
Ramps, bridges and overpasses can freeze before the rest of the road, and drivers should keep a safe distance behind snowplows. [A07]
Why it matters: group winter driving; difficulty medium.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0048]

FACT_ID: sec07-R22 | anchor: A07
In very cold weather, let the engine warm up, keep a full gas tank so the heater can run if stranded, and clear snow from headlights and taillights often. [A07]
Why it matters: group winter driving; difficulty low.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0048]

FACT_ID: sec07-R23 | anchor: A08
Hydroplaning gets worse as speed rises; after driving through puddles, pump the brakes to dry them. [A08]
Why it matters: group rain; difficulty medium.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0049]

FACT_ID: sec07-R24 | anchor: A08
Flash flooding kills more people than any other roadway weather event each year, so never drive around barricades or past road closed signs. [A08]
Why it matters: group flooding; difficulty low.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0049]

FACT_ID: sec07-R25 | anchor: A08
To avoid the glare of oncoming headlights at night, do not look straight into them; focus on the right side of the road instead. [A08]
Why it matters: group night driving; difficulty low.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0049]

FACT_ID: sec07-R26 | anchor: A09
Young adults aged 16 to 29 are at the highest risk of drowsy driving, accounting for 64 percent of fatigue-related crashes. [A09]
Why it matters: group drowsy driving; difficulty medium.
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec07-R27 | anchor: A09
Warning signs of drowsiness include yawning or heavy eyelids, not remembering the last few miles, missing exits, drifting onto rumble strips and failing to hold a steady speed. [A09]
Why it matters: group drowsy driving; difficulty low.
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec07-R28 | anchor: A09
Reading or sending a text takes your eyes off the road for five seconds, which at 55 miles per hour is like driving a football field blind. [A09]
Why it matters: group distracted driving; difficulty low.
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec07-R29 | anchor: A09
About one-third of Indiana traffic deaths come from dangerous driving, meaning crashes caused by aggressive driving, disregarding a signal or speeding. [A09]
Why it matters: group aggressive driving; confusable dangerous versus aggressive.
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec07-R30 | anchor: A10
On gravel, traction is lower, so slow down earlier before turns and stops to avoid skidding. [A10]
Why it matters: group rural roads; difficulty low.
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec07-R31 | anchor: A10
Before the crest of a steep hill, slow down, keep to the right and watch for oncoming vehicles, and never try to pass there. [A10]
Why it matters: group rural roads; link to no-passing rules.
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec07-R32 | anchor: A10
On dusty dirt roads, use low beam headlights so other drivers can see you. [A10]
Why it matters: group rural roads; difficulty low.
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec07-R33 | anchor: A10
Do not stop or park on an interstate shoulder except for an emergency or a disabled vehicle. [A10]
Why it matters: group interstates; difficulty low.
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec07-R34 | anchor: A10
Trucks must stay in the right lane where an interstate has two lanes each way and in the right two lanes where it has three or more. [A10]
Why it matters: group interstates; difficulty medium.
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0051]
